Transformers as Adaptive Kernel Learners across Tasks for In-Context Learning

Zhaiming Shen ††thanks: zhaiming.shen@usu.edu. Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Utah State University, Logan, UT 84322    Alexander Cloninger ††thanks: acloninger@ucsd.edu. Department of Mathematics and Halicioğlu Data Science Institute, University of California, San Diego, La Jolla, CA 92093    Rongjie Lai ††thanks: lairj@purdue.edu. Department of Mathematics, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN 47907    Wenjing Liao ††thanks: wliao60@gatech.edu. School of Mathematics, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA 30332
October 17, 2026
Abstract

Transformers have emerged as a dominant architecture in modern machine learning, with in-context learning (ICL) enabling models to adapt to new tasks by conditioning on prompts, without any parameter updates. To understand the attention mechanism in transformer blocks, a growing line of theoretical work interprets ICL through the lens of classical statistical estimators. Recent works have established a connection between the attention mechanism and kernel methods, while the kernel function is usually assumed to be fixed. In practice, the query and key matrices in the attention mechanism are trained, which allows the attention mechanism to serve as an adaptive kernel method. In this work, we demonstrate that transformers can act as adaptive anisotropic kernel learners. Specifically, we study ICL for low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regressions, and conduct numerical simulations to show that the learned attention scores closely resemble the oracle kernels for these function classes. We then develop a general framework to analyze the generalization error of ICL by connecting transformers to the oracle kernel estimator for each function class. Our theory gives an explicit and constructive implementation of the oracle kernel estimators for these function classes using a wide and shallow transformer architecture, illustrating how the prediction is carried out by the interaction between the query token and the context tokens. Our work complements existing studies by providing numerical and theoretical evidence of how the attention mechanism adapts to anisotropic kernels in both linear and nonlinear settings.

1 Introduction

Introduced by Vaswani17, the transformer architecture has become a cornerstone of modern machine learning, powering significant progress in natural language processing, computer vision, and related fields. In contrast to traditional feedforward and convolutional neural networks, transformers are built upon an attention mechanism that enables each token to attend to all others, dynamically weighting their contributions based on learned relevance. This approach yields representations that are both highly adaptive and sensitive to context. Consequently, transformers underpin many state-of-the-art generative models, including GPT [achiam2023gpt], BERT [devlin2018bert], SORA [videoworldsimulators2024], as well as their subsequent developments.

Beyond their empirical success, transformers exhibit a striking form of in-context learning (ICL), also often refer to as few-shot learning, in which the model effectively adapts to new tasks by conditioning on a sequence of example pairs, referred to as a prompt, at inference time, without any explicit parameter updates [brown2020language; radford2019language; liu2023pre; garg2022can]. This emergent capability has prompted a growing line of work aimed at uncovering its underlying principles. Recent theoretical studies [bai2023transformers; zhang2024trained; von2023transformers; akyurek2022learning; cole2024provable; lu2025transformer] demonstrate that transformers can implicitly implement classical estimation procedures, including least squares, ridge regression, Lasso, generalized linear models, and linear inverse problems. Notably, problems resembling ICL were studied even before the advent of transformers, often referred to as meta-learning or multi-task learning in the literature [baxter2000model; pontil2013excess; maurer2016benefit; tripuraneni2021provable; du2021few].

Beyond linear regimes, a growing body of work has investigated the expressive power, approximation capabilities, and statistical properties of transformers for nonlinear functions and sequence-to-sequence mappings [Yun19; Takakura23; TransformerClassifier; Jiao2026CoD; He2026]. For instance, Yun19 established the universal approximation property of transformers for continuous sequence-to-sequence functions with compact support, albeit with network complexity that can grow exponentially with the input dimension. Extending this line of research, Takakura23 derived approximation and estimation guarantees for sequence-to-sequence mappings on infinite-dimensional domains under anisotropic smoothness assumptions, while TransformerClassifier studied the statistical properties of transformer classifiers under hierarchical composition and Hölder regularity assumptions. More recently, Jiao2026CoD investigated the ability of transformers to overcome the curse of dimensionality in nonlinear function approximation, while He2026 established quantitative approximation bounds for smooth function classes, further characterizing the approximation efficiency and limitations of transformer architectures. Complementary studies [Havrilla24; shen2025transformers; shi2026learning] have demonstrated that transformers can exploit low-dimensional structure, yielding approximation or generalization guarantees governed by intrinsic rather than ambient dimensionality. These works have focused on approximating or learning a fixed target function or mapping, rather than characterizing the ability of a single transformer to learn previously unseen nonlinear functions from in-context examples.

In contrast, in-context learning (ICL) places transformers in a fundamentally different regime, where a single model must implicitly encode and execute a family of learning procedures, adapting to previously unseen tasks through contextual examples without updating its parameters. This paradigm introduces a distinct form of task-level generalization, requiring the model to transfer its learned inference mechanism across different target functions rather than merely generalize to unseen samples from a fixed task. While substantial theoretical progress has been made in understanding linear ICL, extending these results to nonlinear function classes remains an active area of research. Recent studies have demonstrated that transformers can implement learning algorithms, including functional gradient descent, kernel regression, and polynomial regression [li2023transformers; bai2023transformers; Cheng2024; Sun2026; shen2025understanding; hsu2026understanding]. Complementary works have investigated nonlinear feature learning and the training dynamics of transformers [KimSuzuki2024; Li2024Nonlinear], while Kim2024Minimax; Ching2026; shen2025understanding established statistical guarantees for nonparametric ICL over smooth function classes. Beyond finite-dimensional regression and classification, ICL has also been investigated in the context of operator learning [chiu2025context], further broadening its scope to function-space learning problems.

Another important yet less explored direction is understanding how shared structure across tasks can be exploited to reduce learning complexity and improve generalization in the task space [lu2025transformer; cole2026incontext; shi2026transformers]. In inverse linear regression, lu2025transformer showed that a linear transformer can learn a cross-task prior and an effective regularization strategy. cole2026incontext studied in-context operator learning for optimal transport on probability measure spaces and established generalization bounds that quantify the effect of the intrinsic task dimension. For nonlinear task families, shi2026transformers characterized cross-task complexity through covering numbers and constructed transformers that exploit this structure. A generalization error bound is derived in shi2026transformers to demonstrate the context-sample efficiency with low-dimensional cross-task structures. Despite of these theoretical progresses, how transformers learn and adapt to shared cross-task structure remains incompletely understood, both theoretically and computationally.

In this work, we investigate how the attention mechanism adapts to shared cross-task structure in linear and nonlinear regression through the lens of adaptive anisotropic kernels. We demonstrate this kernel perspective through numerical experiments and theoretical analysis in two representative settings: low-rank linear regression and anisotropic kernel regression with noisy observations. Our main contributions are summarized as follows.

  • •

    We investigate the in-context learning behavior of transformers in low-rank linear and multi-index nonlinear regression models. Numerical experiments reveal a strong correlation between the attention scores in the final layer of trained transformers and the underlying ground-truth algorithmic kernels in both settings, providing empirical evidence that transformers can implicitly learn task-specific prediction algorithms.

  • •

    Motivated by these empirical observations, we establish the generalization error bounds for transformer-based ICL in both settings, demonstrating that transformers can implicitly implement low-rank linear regression and anisotropic kernel regression respectively.

  • •

    We provide explicit, step-by-step constructions of wide and shallow transformer architectures that realize the corresponding in-context learning algorithms in both settings. These constructions elucidate how transformers leverage contextual examples to perform task-specific inference without updating their parameters.

The rest of paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the notations and preliminary definitions. In Section 3, we introduce the problem setup for In-Context Learning (ICL) and transformer for ICL. In Section 4 and 5, we illustrate how transformer adapt to the cases such as low-rank linear regression and anisotropic kernel regression, as well as discuss their statistical estimation error for functions in these two classes. We also refer the two regression tasks as low-rank linear model and multi-index model respectively. In Section 6 and Section 7, we rigorously show the generalization error bound for low-rank linear model and multi-index model respectively. Finally, Section 8 concludes the paper by discussing its limitations and potential directions for future research.

Definition 2 (Covering Number).

Let (ℱ,ρ)(\mathcal{F},\rho) be a metric space. For a given ϵ>0\epsilon>0, the covering number 𝒩⁡(ϵ,ℱ,ρ)\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\rho) is the smallest number of balls of radius ϵ\epsilon needed to cover ℱ\mathcal{F}. More precisely,

𝒩(ϵ,ℱ,ρ):=min{N∈ℕ | ∃{f1,f2,…,fN}⊆ℱ,∀f∈ℱ,∃fi such that ρ(f,fi)≤ϵ}.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\epsilon,\mathcal{F},\rho):=\min\{N\in\mathbb{N}\text{ }|\text{ }\exists\{f_{1},f_{2},\dots,f_{N}\}\subseteq\mathcal{F},\ \forall f\in\mathcal{F},\ \exists f_{i}\text{ such that }\rho(f,f_{i})\leq\epsilon\}.
Definition 3 (Attention and Multi-head Attention).

Attention with the Query, Key, Value matrices Q,K,V∈ℝde​m​b​e​d×de​m​b​e​dQ,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{embed}\times d_{embed}} is defined as

AK,Q,V​(H)=V​H​σ​((K​H)⊤​Q​H).\textstyle{\rm A}_{K,Q,V}(H)=VH\sigma((KH)^{\top}QH). (1)

The multi-head attention (MHA) with mm heads is the linear superposition of attentions given by

MHA⁡(H)=∑j=1mVj​H​σ​((Kj​H)⊤​Qj​H)\textstyle{\rm MHA}(H)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}V_{j}H\sigma((K_{j}H)^{\top}Q_{j}H) (2)

with σ\sigma be some activation function to be specified.

A transformer block is a residual composition of the form

B⁡(H)=FFN⁡(MHA⁡(H)+H)+MHA⁡(H)+H.{\rm B}(H)={\rm FFN}({\rm MHA}(H)+H)+{\rm MHA}(H)+H. (3)

where FFN is a feed-forward neural network operating tokenwise on the input.

3 Problem Setup

3.1 In-Context Learning (ICL)

Let 𝐱∈ℝD\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} be a random sample from a distribution ρ𝐱\rho_{\mathbf{x}} supported on a bounded domain Ω⊂ℝD\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{D}. A function f:Ω→ℝf:\Omega\to\mathbb{R} maps a point on Ω\Omega to a real number. Suppose ρf\rho_{f} is a probability distribution in the target function space {f:Ω→ℝ}\{f:\ \Omega\to\mathbb{R}\} and ρf\rho_{f} is supported on a function class ℱ⊂{f:Ω→ℝ}\mathcal{F}\subset\{f:\ \Omega\to\mathbb{R}\}.

Setting 1.

We consider in-context regression where a prompt/task is given as

𝔰={𝐱1,y1,𝐱2,y2,…,𝐱n,yn;𝐱n+1,yn+1}​ with ​yi=f⁡(𝐱i)+ϵi,\mathfrak{s}=\{\mathbf{x}_{1},y_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},y_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n},y_{n};\mathbf{x}_{n+1},y_{n+1}\}\ \text{ with }y_{i}=f(\mathbf{x}_{i})+\epsilon_{i}, (7)

where 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i}’s are i.i.d. samples from ρ𝐱\rho_{\mathbf{x}}, ff is sampled from ρf\rho_{f}, and ϵi\epsilon_{i}’s are i.i.d. Gaussian noise: ϵi∼N⁡(0,σ2)\epsilon_{i}\sim N(0,\sigma^{2}). The goal is to predict f⁡(𝐱n+1)f(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}) from {𝐱1,y1,𝐱2,y2,…,𝐱n,yn;𝐱n+1}\{\mathbf{x}_{1},y_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2},y_{2},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n},y_{n};\mathbf{x}_{n+1}\}. The training data contains Γ\Gamma tasks: 𝔖:={𝔰γ}γ=1Γ\mathfrak{S}:=\{\mathfrak{s}^{\gamma}\}_{\gamma=1}^{\Gamma} where

𝔰γ={𝐱1γ,y1γ,…,𝐱nγ,ynγ;𝐱n+1γ,yn+1γ}​ with ​yiγ=fγ​(𝐱iγ)+ϵiγ,\mathfrak{s}^{\gamma}=\{\mathbf{x}_{1}^{\gamma},y^{\gamma}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n}^{\gamma},y_{n}^{\gamma};\mathbf{x}_{n+1}^{\gamma},y_{n+1}^{\gamma}\}\ \text{ with }y_{i}^{\gamma}=f^{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{i})+\epsilon^{\gamma}_{i},

where {𝐱iγ}i=1,…,n+1γ=1,…,Γ\{\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\gamma}\}_{i=1,\ldots,n+1}^{\gamma=1,\ldots,\Gamma} are i.i.d. samples from the ρ𝐱\rho_{\mathbf{x}}, {fγ}γ=1,…,Γ\{f^{\gamma}\}_{\gamma=1,\ldots,\Gamma} are i.i.d. samples from the ρf\rho_{f}, and {ϵiγ}i=1,…,n+1γ=1,…,Γ\{\epsilon^{\gamma}_{i}\}_{i=1,\ldots,n+1}^{\gamma=1,\ldots,\Gamma} are i.i.d. Gaussian noise.

In Setting 1, nn is the prompt length and Γ\Gamma is the training sample/task size. For a random sample 𝔰\mathfrak{s} in (7) and an in-context regression algorithm denoted by T{{\rm T}}, we define the the risk as the squared prediction error: ℛ𝔰(T):=(T({𝐱i,yi}i=1n};𝐱n+1)−yn+1)2\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}}({{\rm T}}):=\left({{{\rm T}}}(\{\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\};\mathbf{x}_{n+1})-y_{n+1}\right)^{2}. Given the training set 𝔖\mathfrak{S}, we minimize the following empirical risk:

ℛ^𝔖​(Tθ):=1Γ​∑γ=1Γℛ𝔰γ​(Tθ)\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}}({{{\rm T}}}_{\theta}):=\frac{1}{\Gamma}\sum_{\gamma=1}^{\Gamma}\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}^{\gamma}}({{\rm T}}_{\theta}) =1Γ∑γ=1Γ(Tθ({𝐱iγ,yiγ}i=1n};𝐱n+1γ)−yn+1γ)2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Gamma}\sum_{\gamma=1}^{\Gamma}\Big({{{\rm T}}}_{\theta}(\{\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{i},y^{\gamma}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\};\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{n+1})-y^{\gamma}_{n+1}\Big)^{2} (8)

where 𝒯{\mathcal{T}} is a transformer neural network class with the architecture to be specified.

𝔰f={𝐱1,y1,…,𝐱n,yn;𝐱n+1,f⁡(𝐱n+1)},\mathfrak{s}_{f}=\{\mathbf{x}_{1},y_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n},y_{n};\mathbf{x}_{n+1},f(\mathbf{x}_{n+1})\}, (10)

ℛ⁡(T^)=𝔼𝔖​𝔼𝔰f​[ℛ𝔰f​(T^)]\mathcal{R}(\widehat{{{\rm T}}})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{S}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\widehat{{{\rm T}}})\right] (11)

Given an input 𝔰\mathfrak{s}, the transformer first apply PE+E⁡(𝔰){\rm PE}+{\rm E}(\mathfrak{s}) to get an embedding matrix

H=PE+E⁡(𝔰)=[𝐱1⋯𝐱n𝐱n+1y1⋯yn00⋯⋯00⋯⋯0ℐ1⋯⋯ℐn+11⋯⋯1]∈ℝde​m​b​e​d×ℓ=ℝde​m​b​e​d×(n+1).\displaystyle H={\rm PE}+{\rm E}\left(\mathfrak{s}\right)=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}_{1}&\cdots&\mathbf{x}_{n}&\mathbf{x}_{n+1}\\ y_{1}&\cdots&y_{n}&0\\ 0&\cdots&\cdots&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\\ 0&\cdots&\cdots&0\\ \mathcal{I}_{1}&\cdots&\cdots&\mathcal{I}_{n+1}\\ 1&\cdots&\cdots&1\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{embed}\times\ell}=\mathbb{R}^{d_{embed}\times(n+1)}. Remark 1.

Since Gaussian noise is unbounded, the input embedding matrix HH and the transformer output Tθ​(⋅){\rm T}_{\theta}(\cdot) may be unbounded as well. We therefore truncate the network values so that both remain bounded with high probability. Without loss of generality, we assume that our subsequent analysis is carried out under this truncation for both the input and output.

In (14), we fix ℓ=n+1\ell=n+1, and we regard each column as a token, whose embedding dimension is de​m​b​e​dd_{embed}. We use HH as the input for the first layer of transformer B1{\rm B}_{1}, then successively as input for B2{\rm B}_{2}, B3{\rm B}_{3}, ⋯\cdots, etc,. In section 6 and section 7, we will show step-by-step how to construct a specific transformer so it can implement desirable output.

Our goal next is to illustrate via both mathematical formulation and numerical experiments how transformer can adaptively learn anisotropic kernel functions by taking HH as an input for the cases of low-rank linear regression and anisotropic kernel regression with noisy responses.

4 Transformer as an Adaptive Kernel Learner

The attention mechanism in transformers bears a strong resemblance to kernel methods. Both rely on pairwise interactions to adaptively aggregate information across inputs: kernel methods weight inputs through a kernel function, while transformers do so through attention scores. Motivated by this connection, we study transformer based ICL through the lens of kernel methods.

Given a random sample 𝔰\mathfrak{s} in (7), the empirical oracle kernel estimator in its most general form is

𝒦⁡(𝔰):=∑i=1nK⁡(𝐱n+1,𝐱i)​yi\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s}):={\sum_{i=1}^{n}K(\mathbf{x}_{n+1},\mathbf{x}_{i})y_{i}} (15)

where K⁡(𝐱n+1,𝐱i)K(\mathbf{x}_{n+1},\mathbf{x}_{i}) represents an interaction kernel between the query 𝐱n+1\mathbf{x}_{n+1} and the prompt point 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i}. In practice, the interaction kernel can take different forms depending on the function class ℱ\mathcal{F}.

In this paper, we establish a connection between transformers and adaptive kernel methods and provide a general framework for analyzing the generalization error of transformer-based ICL. For a function class ℱ\mathcal{F} of interest, if an oracle kernel estimator 𝒦\mathcal{K} exists and can be well approximated by a transformer neural network, our framework enables the development of corresponding generalization guarantees. In particular, we summarize several classical function classes and their corresponding oracle interaction kernels in Table 1. The notation [⋅]†[\cdot]^{\dagger} denotes matrix pseudo-inverse, which coincides with the inverse whenever the matrix is invertible.

For these classical function classes, we can construct a transformer T∗{{\rm T}}^{*} to approximate the associated oracle kernel estimator 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Specifically, we focus on illustrating the cases for low-rank linear model and multi-index model in Section 4.1 and Section 4.2 respectively. Then we analyze the generalization error of transformer-based ICL via a bias–variance decomposition in Section 5, and discuss the statistical error in Sections 5.1 and 5.2.

4.1 Low-rank Linear Model

We first consider linear functions that share a low-dimensional linear structure across different tasks. Let W∈ℝD×rW\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times r} be a fixed matrix with orthonormal columns, which represent a low-dimensional task subspace. The low-rank linear function class

ℱLinear,W:={f: f(𝐱)=𝐰⊤𝐱 for some 𝐰=W𝜷, with 𝜷∼ρ𝜷 in ℝr satisfying ∥𝜷∥2≤β}.\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{{\rm Linear},W}:=\{f:\text{ }f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}\text{ for some }\mathbf{w}=W\bm{\beta},\text{ with }\bm{\beta}\sim\rho_{\bm{\beta}}\text{ in }\mathbb{R}^{r}\text{ satisfying }\|\bm{\beta}\|_{2}\leq\beta\}. (16)

exhibits a low-dimensional task structure characterized by the subspace WW. In ℱLinear,W\mathcal{F}_{{\rm Linear},W}, the task subspace WW exists, but is unknown as a prior information. The information about WW is supposed to be learned cross all training tasks. See Figure 1 for an illustration of this function class.

Suppose X=[𝐱1,⋯,𝐱n]⊤∈ℝn×DX=[\mathbf{x}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{x}_{n}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times D}. For convenience, we introduce Z=[𝐳1,⋯,𝐳n]⊤∈ℝn×rZ=[\mathbf{z}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{z}_{n}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} with 𝐳i:=W⊤​𝐱i∈ℝr\mathbf{z}_{i}:=W^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{r} for i=1,⋯,ni=1,\cdots,n, and Z=X​W∈ℝn×rZ=XW\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}. The uncentered population covariance matrix of the random vector 𝐳:=W⊤​𝐱\mathbf{z}:=W^{\top}\mathbf{x} when 𝐱∼ρ𝐱\mathbf{x}\sim\rho_{\mathbf{x}} is Σ𝐳:=𝔼⁡[𝐳𝐳⊤]=𝔼𝐱∼ρ𝐱​[W⊤​𝐱𝐱⊤​W]∈ℝr×r\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}}:=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}\mathbf{z}^{\top}]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\rho_{\mathbf{x}}}[W^{\top}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}W]\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}.

The population covariance matrix Σ𝐳\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}} positive semidefinite but may not be full rank. In the case that Σ𝐳\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}} is not full rank, we use Σ𝐳†\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}}^{\dagger} to indicate its pseudo-inverse. Suppose the population level covariance Σ𝐳\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}} has rank kk, our oracle kernel estimator (17) will be in terms of the kk-th order truncated pseudo-inverse [⋅]k†[\cdot]^{\dagger}_{k} as defined in Definition 1.

Let 𝐲=[y1,⋯,yn]⊤∈ℝn\mathbf{y}=[y_{1},\cdots,y_{n}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. The function f⁡(𝐱)=𝐰⊤​𝐱=(W​𝜷)⊤​𝐱=𝐱⊤​W​𝜷f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}=(W\bm{\beta})^{\top}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^{\top}W\bm{\beta} can be estimated from the linear system X​W​𝜷=𝐲XW\bm{\beta}=\mathbf{y} with the least squares solution 𝜷^=[W⊤​X⊤​X​W]k†​W⊤​X⊤​𝐲\widehat{\bm{\beta}}=[W^{\top}X^{\top}XW]_{k}^{\dagger}W^{\top}X^{\top}\mathbf{y} so that f⁡(𝐱n+1)f(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}) can be approximated by the oracle kernel estimator

𝒦⁡(𝔰)=𝒦⁡(𝔰f)\displaystyle\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s})=\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s}_{f}) =𝐱n+1⊤​W​[W⊤​X⊤​X​W]k†​W⊤​X⊤​𝐲\displaystyle=\mathbf{x}_{n+1}^{\top}W[W^{\top}X^{\top}XW]_{k}^{\dagger}W^{\top}X^{\top}\mathbf{y}
=∑i=1n(W⊤​𝐱n+1)⊤​[W⊤​X⊤​X​W]k†⏟r×r​(W⊤​𝐱i)​yi=∑i=1nK⁡(𝐱n+1,𝐱i)​yi\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(W^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{n+1})^{\top}\underbrace{[W^{\top}X^{\top}XW]_{k}^{\dagger}}_{r\times r}(W^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{i})y_{i}={\sum_{i=1}^{n}K(\mathbf{x}_{n+1},\mathbf{x}_{i})y_{i}} (17)

which can be expressed in the kernel form of (15) with the linear interaction kernel

K⁡(𝐱n+1,𝐱i)=(W⊤​𝐱n+1)⊤​[W⊤​X⊤​X​W]k†⏟r×r​(W⊤​𝐱i).K(\mathbf{x}_{n+1},\mathbf{x}_{i})=(W^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{n+1})^{\top}\underbrace{[W^{\top}X^{\top}XW]_{k}^{\dagger}}_{r\times r}(W^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{i}). (18)

The low-rank linear model directly connects to the ordinary linear model as well as low-rank linear feature model, where we briefly showcase their connections in Appendix B. It is worth pointing out the previous work in hsu2026understanding studies ICL in the low-rank linear feature model setup when the feature map is taken to be polynomial or spline basis.

We next show that transformer does adaptively learn the low-rank structure in their kernel representation via simulated experiments.

Experiments for low-rank linear model.

For low-rank linear function class ℱLinear,W\mathcal{F}_{{\rm Linear},W}, we consider f⁡(𝐱)=𝐰⊤​𝐱f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x} for 𝐱∈[0,1]5\mathbf{x}\in[0,1]^{5} with 𝐰=W​β∈ℝ5\mathbf{w}=W\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{5}. Here we uniform randomly sample β\beta from [0,1]2[0,1]^{2}, and each realization of β\beta is a learning task. W∈ℝ5×2W\in\mathbb{R}^{5\times 2} is chosen as an orthonormal matrix across all the tasks.

Next, we train the transformer to learn this function class. Top row of Figure 2 plots the attention scores (after sorting from the highest to the lowest value) in the last layer of the trained transformer and compares it against the low-rank linear kernel function (18) (sorted according to the sorting index for attention scores), which demonstrates a strong correlation between the two quantities. Bottom row of Figure 2 plots the distribution of the Pearson correlation values between the last layer of the trained transformer and different kernel functions.

Table 2 further confirms that the low-rank linear kernel (18) has the largest correlation with the transformer model final layer attention score. Note that the anisotropic Gaussian kernel achieves a comparable Pearson correlation coefficient, due to both the low-rank linear and anisotropic Gaussian kernels can capture the same underlying directional structure. Further experimental details are provided in Appendix C.

4.2 Multi-index Model

We next consider an anisotropic regular function model, i.e., multi-index model, a class of nonlinear function models which share some low-dimensional task features. The multi-index model for a fixed subspace U∈ℝD×rU\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times r}:

ℱMI,U:={f:Ω→ℝ |\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{{\rm MI},U}:=\{f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\text{ }| ​f​(𝐱)=g⁡(U⊤​𝐱)​ for some ​α​-Hölder ​g:ℝr→ℝ​ with Hölder constant\displaystyle\text{ }f(\mathbf{x})=g(U^{\top}\mathbf{x})\text{ for some }\alpha\text{-H\"{o}lder }g:\mathbb{R}^{r}\to\mathbb{R}\text{ with H\"{o}lder constant}
no larger than L, and ∥f∥L∞​(Ω)≤R}\displaystyle\text{ no larger than }L,\text{ and }\|f\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq R\} (19)

Here all tasks share the same low-dimensional task space UU. Without loss of generality, we assume the columns of UU are orthonormal. See Figure 3 for an illustration of this function class.

If we use the classical Nadaraya–Watson kernel estimator [nadaraya1964estimating; watson1964smooth] to estimate ff through gg, we get the corresponding oracle kernel estimator for ℱMI,U\mathcal{F}_{{\rm MI},U} is given by

𝒦⁡(𝔰)=𝒦⁡(𝔰f)=∑i=1nyi​Kh​(𝐱n+1−𝐱i)∑i=1nKh​(𝐱n+1−𝐱i)=∑i=1nK⁡(𝐱n+1,𝐱i)​yi.\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s})=\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s}_{f})=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{i}K_{h}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\mathbf{x}_{i})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}K_{h}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\mathbf{x}_{i})}={\sum_{i=1}^{n}K(\mathbf{x}_{n+1},\mathbf{x}_{i})y_{i}}. (20)

One common choice is Kh(𝐱)=e−∥𝐱∥22/h2K_{h}(\mathbf{x})=e^{-\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}^{2}/h^{2}}, with a proper choice of the kernel bandwidth hh. With this choice KhK_{h} for the estimation of gg, the corresponding interaction kernel for the estimation of ff can be written as

K⁡(𝐱n+1,𝐱i)=e−∥U⊤(𝐱n+1−𝐱i)∥2/h2∑i=1ne−∥U⊤(𝐱n+1−𝐱i)∥2/h2,K(\mathbf{x}_{n+1},\mathbf{x}_{i})=\frac{e^{-\|U^{\top}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\mathbf{x}_{i})\|^{2}/h^{2}}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}e^{-\|U^{\top}(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-\mathbf{x}_{i})\|^{2}/h^{2}}}, (21)

when the subspace UU is known. In practice, the subspace UU is unknown, and needs to be learned from training data.

The multi-index model naturally works as a generalization of the single-index model as well as the class of isotropic regular function, we briefly mention their connection in the Appendix B. It is worth pointing out the work in shen2025understanding studies ICL when the Nadaraya–Watson kernel is set to be isotropic when U=IU=I.

We next demonstrate via simulated experiments that transformer does adaptively learn the anisotropic structure in their kernel representation.

Experiments for multi-index models

For function class ℱMI,U\mathcal{F}_{{\rm MI},U}, we consider f⁡(𝐱)=g⁡(U⊤​𝐱)f(\mathbf{x})=g(U^{\top}\mathbf{x}), for 𝐱∈[0,1]5\mathbf{x}\in[0,1]^{5}, where gg is a Legendre polynomial on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} with six random coefficients, i.e., g⁡(x,y)=c0​P0​(x,y)+c1​P1​(x,y)+c2​P2​(x,y)+c3​P3​(x,y)+c4​P4​(x,y)+c5​P5​(x,y)g(x,y)=c_{0}P_{0}(x,y)+c_{1}P_{1}(x,y)+c_{2}P_{2}(x,y)+c_{3}P_{3}(x,y)+c_{4}P_{4}(x,y)+c_{5}P_{5}(x,y), where c0,c1,c2,c3,c4,c5c_{0},c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4},c_{5} are uniformly random sampled from [0,1][0,1]. Each realization of c0,c1,c2,c3,c4,c5c_{0},c_{1},c_{2},c_{3},c_{4},c_{5} is a learning task. In ℱMI,U\mathcal{F}_{{\rm MI},U}, we keep U∈ℝ5×2U\in\mathbb{R}^{5\times 2} as a random but fixed orthonormal matrix across all tasks.

Next, we train the transformer to learn this function class. Top row of Figure 4 plots the attention scores (after sorting from the highest to the lowest value) in the last layer of the trained transformer and compares it against the anisotropic Gaussian kernel function (21) (sorted according to the sorting index for attention scores), which demonstrates a strong correlation between the two quantities. Bottom row of Figure 4 plots the distribution of the Pearson correlation values between the last layer of the trained transformer and different kernel functions.

Table 3 further confirms that the anisotropic Gaussian kernel (21) has the largest correlation with the transformer model final layer attention score. Further experimental details are provided in Appendix C.

5 Error Analysis Connecting Transformers and Kernel Algorithms

To establish the generalization error for both the low-rank linear model and the multi-index model using transformer, let us demonstrate the generalization error decomposition as well as the statistical error estimation in Section 5.1 and Section 5.2.

We first decompose the mean squared generalization error in (11) via a bias–variance decomposition. For the sake of error analysis, we define 𝔖f:={𝔰fγ}γ=1Γ\mathfrak{S}_{f}:=\{\mathfrak{s}_{f}^{\gamma}\}_{\gamma=1}^{\Gamma} where

𝔰fγ={𝐱1γ,y1γ,…,𝐱nγ,ynγ;𝐱n+1γ,fγ​(𝐱n+1γ)},\mathfrak{s}^{\gamma}_{f}=\{\mathbf{x}_{1}^{\gamma},y^{\gamma}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{n}^{\gamma},y_{n}^{\gamma};\mathbf{x}_{n+1}^{\gamma},f^{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{n+1})\},

and the empirical risk without noise

ℛ^𝔖f(Tθ):=1Γ∑γ=1Γℛ𝔰fγ(Tθ)=1Γ∑γ=1Γ(Tθ({𝐱iγ,yiγ}i=1n};𝐱n+1γ)−fγ(𝐱n+1γ))2.\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}_{f}}({{{\rm T}}}_{\theta}):=\frac{1}{\Gamma}\sum_{\gamma=1}^{\Gamma}\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}^{\gamma}_{f}}({{\rm T}}_{\theta})=\frac{1}{\Gamma}\sum_{\gamma=1}^{\Gamma}\Big({{{\rm T}}}_{\theta}(\{\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{i},y^{\gamma}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\};\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{n+1})-f^{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{n+1})\Big)^{2}. (22)

We can then decompose the squared generalization error of T^\widehat{{\rm T}} on a random test sample 𝔰f\mathfrak{s}_{f} as follows:

ℛ𝔰f​(T^)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\widehat{{\rm T}}) =ℛ𝔰f​(T^)−ℛ^𝔖f​(T^)⏟III+ℛ^𝔖f​(T^)−ℛ^𝔖​(T^)⏟V+ℛ^𝔖​(T^)−ℛ^𝔖​(T∗)⏟≤0\displaystyle=\underbrace{{\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\widehat{{\rm T}})}-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}_{f}}(\widehat{{\rm T}})}_{\rm III}+\underbrace{\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}_{f}}(\widehat{{\rm T}})-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}}(\widehat{{\rm T}})}_{\rm V}+\underbrace{{\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}}(\widehat{{\rm T}})-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}}({{\rm T}}^{*})}}_{\rm\leq 0}
+ℛ^𝔖​(T∗)−ℛ^𝔖f​(T∗)⏟VI+ℛ^𝔖f​(T∗)−ℛ𝔰f​(T∗)⏟IV+ℛ𝔰f​(T∗)−2​ℛ𝔰f​(𝒦)⏟II+2​ℛ𝔰f​(𝒦)⏟I,\displaystyle+\underbrace{\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}}({{\rm T}}^{*})-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}_{f}}({{\rm T}}^{*})}_{\rm VI}+\underbrace{\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}_{f}}({{\rm T}}^{*})-\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}({{\rm T}}^{*})}_{\rm IV}+\underbrace{{\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}({{\rm T}}^{*})}-2{\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\mathcal{K})}}_{\rm II}+\underbrace{2{\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\mathcal{K})}}_{\rm I}, (23)

where T∗{{\rm T}}^{*} is a transformer network which approximates the oracle kernel algorithm 𝒦{\mathcal{K}} in (15). Notice that ℛ^𝔖​(T^)−ℛ^𝔖​(T∗)≤0{\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}}(\widehat{{\rm T}})-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}}({{\rm T}}^{*})}\leq 0 since T^\widehat{{\rm T}} is the minimizer of ℛ^𝔖\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}} given in (8). After taking expectations testing and training samples, we can decompose the mean squared generalization error in (11) as:

ℛ⁡(T^)=\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\widehat{{\rm T}})= 𝔼𝔖​𝔼𝔰f​[ℛ𝔰f​(T^)]≤𝔼𝔰f​[2​ℛ𝔰f​(𝒦)]⏟I\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{S}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\widehat{{\rm T}})\right]\leq\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}\left[2\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\mathcal{K})\right]}_{{\rm I}} (24)
+𝔼𝔰f​[ℛ𝔰f​(T∗)−2​ℛ𝔰f​(𝒦)]⏟II\displaystyle+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}({{\rm T}}^{*})-2\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\mathcal{K})\right]}_{\rm II} (25)
+𝔼𝔖​(𝔼𝔰f​[ℛ𝔰f​(T^)]−ℛ^𝔖f​(T^))⏟III+𝔼𝔖​(ℛ^𝔖f​(T∗)−𝔼𝔰f​[ℛ𝔰f​(T∗)])⏟IV\displaystyle+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{S}}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\widehat{{\rm T}})\right]-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}_{f}}(\widehat{{\rm T}})\right)}_{{\rm III}}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{S}}\Big(\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}_{f}}({{\rm T}}^{*})-\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}({{\rm T}}^{*})\right]\Big)}_{{\rm IV}} (26)
+𝔼𝔖​[ℛ^𝔖f​(T^)−ℛ^𝔖​(T^)]⏟V+𝔼𝔖​[ℛ^𝔖​(T∗)−ℛ^𝔖f​(T∗)]⏟VI.\displaystyle+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{S}}\left[\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}_{f}}(\widehat{{\rm T}})-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}}(\widehat{{\rm T}})\right]}_{\rm V}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{S}}\left[\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}}({{\rm T}}^{*})-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{\mathfrak{S}_{f}}({{\rm T}}^{*})\right]}_{\rm VI}. (27)

In this error decomposition, the term I{\rm I} represents the error given by the oracle kernel algorithm, the term II{\rm II} represents the transformer network approximation error for the oracle kernel algorithm. The terms III{\rm III} and IV{\rm IV} correspond to statistical estimation error by transformers, which depends on the transformer network complexity, and the terms V{\rm V} and VI{\rm VI} correspond to the statistical error induced by the noise on the output. In Sections 5.1 and 5.2, we will analyze the statistical errors in the terms III - VI, which depend on the transformer network class. The approximation errors in the terms I - II depend on the function class ℱ\mathcal{F}, which will be analyzed in Section 6 for low-rank linear functions and in Section 7 for nonlinear multi-index functions.

5.1 Statistical Error of Transformers

To bound the statistical error terms in III{\rm III} and IV{\rm IV} in (26), we invoke the standard statistical error analysis techniques such as Rademacher complexity and Dudley entropy integral [dudley1967sizes].

For each sample, the loss function we considered is the squared loss

ℒ𝔰f​(T)=(T⁡({𝐱i,yi}i=1n,𝐱n+1)−f⁡(𝐱n+1))2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}({{\rm T}})=({{\rm T}}(\{\mathbf{x}_{i},y_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};\mathbf{x}_{n+1})-f(\mathbf{x}_{n+1}))^{2}.

and the Rademacher complexity of ℒ∘𝒯\mathcal{L}\circ{\mathcal{T}} with respect to 𝔖f\mathfrak{S}_{f} is

Rad𝔖f​(ℒ∘𝒯):=1Γ​𝔼𝝃∼{±1}Γ​[supT∈𝒯∑γ=1Γξγ​(T⁡({𝐱iγ,yiγ}i=1n,𝐱n+1γ)−fγ​(𝐱n+1γ))2].{{\rm Rad}}_{\mathfrak{S}_{f}}(\mathcal{L}\circ{\mathcal{T}}):=\frac{1}{\Gamma}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\xi}\sim\{\pm 1\}^{\Gamma}}\left[\sup_{{{\rm T}}\in{\mathcal{T}}}\sum_{\gamma=1}^{\Gamma}\xi_{\gamma}\Big({{\rm T}}(\{\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{i},y^{\gamma}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{n+1})-f^{\gamma}(\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{n+1})\Big)^{2}\right]. (28)

Lemma 1 below establishes the bound for statistical errors III{\rm III} and IV{\rm IV}. We defer its proof to Appendix D.1.

Lemma 1.

Let 𝒯{\mathcal{T}} be the transformer network class defined in (13) and 𝒩(δ,ℒ∘𝒯,∥⋅∥L∞)\mathcal{N}(\delta,\mathcal{L}\circ\mathcal{T},\|\cdot\|_{L^{\infty}}) be the covering number of the function class ℒ∘𝒯\mathcal{L}\circ{\mathcal{T}} under the L∞L^{\infty} norm. Then

III+IV≤4infϵ>0(2ϵ+12Γ∫ϵ4​R2log𝒩(δ,ℒ∘𝒯,∥⋅∥L∞) dδ).{\rm III}+{\rm IV}\leq 4\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left(2\epsilon+\frac{12}{\sqrt{\Gamma}}\int_{\epsilon}^{4R^{2}}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}(\delta,\mathcal{L}\circ\mathcal{T},\|\cdot\|_{L^{\infty}})}\text{ }d\delta\right). (29)

5.2 Statistical Error Induced by Noise

For the statistical errors induced by noise in V{\rm V} and VI{\rm VI}, we can show that

V+VI≤2​𝔼𝔖​[𝒢𝔖​(ℒ′∘𝒯)],\displaystyle{\rm V}+{\rm VI}\leq 2\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{S}}[\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{S}}(\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\circ{\mathcal{T}})], (30)

where ℒ′​(T∘𝔰γ):=T⁡({𝐱iγ,yiγ}i=1n,𝐱n+1γ)\mathcal{L}^{\prime}({{\rm T}}\circ\mathfrak{s}^{\gamma}):={{\rm T}}(\{\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{i},y^{\gamma}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{n+1}), and 𝒢𝔖​(ℒ′∘𝒯)\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{S}}(\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\circ{\mathcal{T}}) is the Gaussian complexity defined as

𝒢𝔖​(ℒ′∘𝒯):=1Γ​𝔼{ϵn+1γ}γ=1Γ​supT∈𝒯[∑γ=1Γϵn+1γ​(T⁡({𝐱iγ,yiγ}i=1n,𝐱n+1γ))].\mathcal{G}_{\mathfrak{S}}(\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\circ{\mathcal{T}}):=\frac{1}{\Gamma}\mathbb{E}_{\{\epsilon_{n+1}^{\gamma}\}_{\gamma=1}^{\Gamma}}\sup_{{\rm T}\in{\mathcal{T}}}\left[\sum_{\gamma=1}^{\Gamma}\epsilon_{n+1}^{\gamma}\Big({{\rm T}}(\{\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{i},y^{\gamma}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n};\mathbf{x}^{\gamma}_{n+1})\Big)\right]. (31)

This leads to Lemma 2 which establishes the bound for the statistical errors in V{\rm V} and VI{\rm VI}. We defer the derivation of (30) and the proof of Lemma 2 to Appendix D.2.

Lemma 2.

Let 𝒯{\mathcal{T}} be the transformer network class defined in (13) and 𝒩(δ,ℒ′∘𝒯,∥⋅∥L∞)\mathcal{N}(\delta,\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\circ\mathcal{T},\|\cdot\|_{L^{\infty}}) be the covering number of the function class ℒ′∘𝒯\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\circ{\mathcal{T}} under the L∞L^{\infty} norm. Then

V+VI≤4σlog⁡(Γ)⋅infϵ>0(2ϵ+12Γ∫ϵRlog𝒩(δ,ℒ′∘𝒯,∥⋅∥L∞) dδ).{\rm V}+{\rm VI}\leq 4\sigma\sqrt{\log(\Gamma)}\cdot\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left(2\epsilon+\frac{12}{\sqrt{\Gamma}}\int_{\epsilon}^{R}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}(\delta,\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\circ\mathcal{T},\|\cdot\|_{L^{\infty}})}\text{ }d\delta\right). (32)

Transformer Network Covering Number.

To further bound the covering numbers appearing in Lemmas 1 and 2, we establish a bound on the covering number of the transformer network class 𝒯{\mathcal{T}} in Lemma 3. The proof follows the argument of Lemma 4 in shen2025understanding and we omitted the proof details here.

Lemma 3.

For a transformer class 𝒯⁡(LT,mT,de​m​b​e​d,ℓ,LFFN,wFFN,R,κ)\mathcal{T}(L_{\rm T},m_{\rm T},d_{embed},\ell,L_{\rm FFN},w_{\rm FFN},R,\kappa) with input ‖H‖∞,∞≤u\|H\|_{\infty,\infty}\leq u. Let δ>0\delta>0, then the covering number of ℒ∘𝒯\mathcal{L}\circ{\mathcal{T}} satisfies

𝒩(δ,ℒ∘𝒯,∥⋅∥L∞)≤(2LT2+4​LFFN​u3​LT​de​m​b​e​d18​LT2​LFFN​κ6​LT2​LFFN+1​mTLT2​ℓLT2​Rδ)PT,\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\delta,\mathcal{L}\circ{\mathcal{T}},\|\cdot\|_{L^{\infty}})\leq\left(\frac{2^{L^{2}_{\rm T}+4}L_{\rm FFN}u^{3L_{\rm T}}d_{embed}^{18L_{\rm T}^{2}L_{\rm FFN}}\kappa^{6L_{\rm T}^{2}L_{\rm FFN}+1}m_{\rm T}^{L_{\rm T}^{2}}\ell^{L_{\rm T}^{2}}R}{\delta}\right)^{P_{\rm T}},

and the covering number of ℒ′∘𝒯\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\circ{\mathcal{T}} satisfies

𝒩(δ,ℒ′∘𝒯,∥⋅∥L∞)≤(2LT2+2​LFFN​u3​LT​de​m​b​e​d18​LT2​LFFN​κ6​LT2​LFFN+1​mTLT2​ℓLT2δ)PT,\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(\delta,\mathcal{L}^{\prime}\circ{\mathcal{T}},\|\cdot\|_{L^{\infty}})\leq\left(\frac{2^{L^{2}_{\rm T}+2}L_{\rm FFN}u^{3L_{\rm T}}d_{embed}^{18L_{\rm T}^{2}L_{\rm FFN}}\kappa^{6L_{\rm T}^{2}L_{\rm FFN}+1}m_{\rm T}^{L_{\rm T}^{2}}\ell^{L_{\rm T}^{2}}}{\delta}\right)^{P_{\rm T}},

where PT=de​m​b​e​d​(D+1)+LT​(3​de​m​b​e​d2​mT+LFFN​wFFN2)P_{\rm T}=d_{embed}(D+1)+L_{\rm T}(3d_{embed}^{2}m_{\rm T}+L_{\rm FFN}w_{\rm FFN}^{2}).

Our next goal is to study the approximation errors I and II for different function classes ℱ\mathcal{F}. In particular, we will consider low-rank linear functions in Section 6 and nonlinear multi-index functions in Section 7, with a focus on leveraging a low-dimensional task space which is shared for all prompts.

6 ICL Generalization Error for Low-rank Linear Model

In this section, we study the approximation error I{\rm I} and II{\rm II} for the low-rank linear function class ℱLinear,W\mathcal{F}_{{\rm Linear},W} in the ICL setup. We first show that the transformer can approximate the low-rank linear kernel estimator 𝒦⁡(𝔰)\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s}) in (17), and then we bound its mean squared generalization error ℛ⁡(T^)\mathcal{R}(\widehat{{\rm T}}).

Our theory is built on the following assumptions. The first assumption is about the function class.

Assumption 1 (Function Class).

Let β>0\beta>0, W∈ℝD×rW\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times r} be a fixed matrix such that W⊤​W=IW^{\top}W=I, and ρ𝛃\rho_{\bm{\beta}} be a distribution in ℝr\mathbb{R}^{r} supported within {𝛃:‖𝛃‖2≤β}\{\bm{\beta}:\|\bm{\beta}\|_{2}\leq\beta\}. Suppose the function class ℱ\mathcal{F} is the low-rank linear function class in (16) such that

ℱ=ℱLinear,W:={f: f(𝐱)=𝐰⊤𝐱 for some 𝐰=W𝜷, with 𝜷∼ρ𝜷 in ℝr satisfying ∥𝜷∥2≤β},\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}_{{\rm Linear},W}:=\{f:\text{ }f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}\text{ for some }\mathbf{w}=W\bm{\beta},\text{ with }\bm{\beta}\sim\rho_{\bm{\beta}}\text{ in }\mathbb{R}^{r}\text{ satisfying }\|\bm{\beta}\|_{2}\leq\beta\},

and ρf\rho_{f} is the distribution in ℱ\mathcal{F} induced by the distribution ρ𝛃\rho_{\bm{\beta}}.

For convenience, we introduce Z=[𝐳1,⋯,𝐳n]⊤∈ℝn×rZ=[\mathbf{z}_{1},\cdots,\mathbf{z}_{n}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r} with 𝐳i:=W⊤​𝐱i∈ℝr\mathbf{z}_{i}:=W^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{r} for i=1,⋯,ni=1,\cdots,n. Then Z=X​W∈ℝn×rZ=XW\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}. The uncentered population covariance matrix of the random vector 𝐳:=W⊤​𝐱\mathbf{z}:=W^{\top}\mathbf{x} when 𝐱∼ρ𝐱\mathbf{x}\sim\rho_{\mathbf{x}} is Σ𝐳:=𝔼⁡[𝐳𝐳⊤]=𝔼𝐱∼ρ𝐱​[W⊤​𝐱𝐱⊤​W]∈ℝr×r\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}}:=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{z}\mathbf{z}^{\top}]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim\rho_{\mathbf{x}}}[W^{\top}\mathbf{x}\mathbf{x}^{\top}W]\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}.

Notice that Σ𝐳\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}} positive semidefinite. In case that Σ𝐳\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}} is not full rank, we use Σ𝐳†\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}}^{\dagger} to indicate its pesudo-inverse. Our second assumption is about the boundedness of input 𝐱\mathbf{x}, and low-rankness of the covariance matrix over transformed input 𝐳\mathbf{z}.

Assumption 2 (Input Distribution).

Let b>0b>0 and W∈ℝD×rW\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times r} be a fixed matrix such that W⊤​W=IW^{\top}W=I. The input distribution ρ𝐱\rho_{\mathbf{x}} is supported within the ball Ω={𝐱:‖𝐱‖2≤b}\Omega=\{\mathbf{x}:\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}\leq b\}. The convariance matrix Σ𝐳\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}} has rank kk: λ1​(Σ𝐳)≥…≥λk​(Σ𝐳)>λk+1​(Σ𝐳)=⋯=λr​(Σ𝐳)=0\lambda_{1}(\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}})\geq\ldots\geq\lambda_{k}(\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}})>\lambda_{k+1}(\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}})=\cdots=\lambda_{r}(\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}})=0 and the top kk nonzero-eigenvalues are bounded away from 00: there exists τ>0\tau>0 such that

‖Σ𝐳†‖2=λ1​(Σ𝐳†)=1λk​(Σ𝐳)≤τ.\|\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}}^{\dagger}\|_{2}={\lambda_{1}(\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}}^{\dagger})}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{k}(\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}})}\leq\tau. (33)

It is worth noting that existing studies have primarily focused on either full-rank linear models [bai2023transformers; zhang2024trained] or low-rank models in which the shared structure is characterized solely by the rank of WW [maurer2016benefit; tripuraneni2021provable]. Our framework extends these settings by simultaneously accounting for the rank rr of the shared representation WW and the effective rank kk of its interaction with the input data XX. In particular, our analysis naturally recovers the cases r=Dr=D and k=rk=r as special cases.

Intuitively, Assumption 2 assumes that among all the kk identifiable directions in ℝr\mathbb{R}^{r}, there is no direction that is negligible. Under Assumption 2 with ‖𝐱‖2≤b\|\mathbf{x}\|_{2}\leq b and Assumption 1 with ‖𝜷‖2≤β\|\bm{\beta}\|_{2}\leq\beta, it is easy to see that all functions in ℱ\mathcal{F} are bounded by ‖f‖L∞​(Ω)=sup‖𝜷‖2≤β|(W​𝜷)⊤​𝐱|≤b​β\|f\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}=\sup_{\|\bm{\beta}\|_{2}\leq\beta}|(W\bm{\beta})^{\top}\mathbf{x}|\leq b\beta.

Further, let us denote Σ^𝐳:=Z⊤​Zn\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}:=\frac{Z^{\top}Z}{n} as the empirical covariance matrix. When the sample size nn is large, it is often the case Σ^𝐳≈Σ𝐳\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}\approx\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}}. We consider a good event ℰ\mathcal{E} when the difference between Σ^𝐳\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}} and Σ𝐳\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}} is bounded by 14​τ\frac{1}{4\tau}:

ℰ:={∥Σ^𝐳−Σ𝐳∥2≤14​τ}.\mathcal{E}:=\{\|\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathbf{z}}-\Sigma_{\mathbf{z}}\|_{2}\leq\frac{1}{4\tau}\}. (34)

Our goal next is to bound the errors I{\rm I} and II{\rm II} in Section 6.1 and Section 6.2 on the good event ℰ\mathcal{E}. Then we combine all the errors to get an error bound for ℛ⁡(T^)\mathcal{R}(\widehat{\rm T}) in Section 6.3.

6.1 Transformer Approximates the Low-rank Linear Kernel

Our goal in this subsection is to demonstrate that, under the good event ℰ\mathcal{E}, a transformer can approximate the low-rank linear kernel oracle estimator 𝒦⁡(𝔰)\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s}) defined in (17). Specifically, in Lemma 4, we provide an explicit step-by-step construction of a linear transformer that uses the embedding matrix (14) to approximate the low-rank linear kernel estimator 𝒦⁡(𝔰)\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s}) to arbitrary prescribed accuracy. Note that such connection between low-rank linear kernel and transformer is also validated by the numerical experiment shown in Section 4.1.

Lemma 4.

Suppose the input satisfies Assumption 2 and the target function class satisfies Assumption 1. Then under Setting 1, there exists a transformer network T∗∈𝒯{\rm T}^{*}\in\mathcal{T} with parameters

de​m​b​e​d=2D+6, ℓ=n+1, LT=2, mT=1,\displaystyle d_{embed}=2D+6,\text{ }\ell=n+1,\text{ }L_{\rm T}=2,\text{ }m_{\rm T}=1,
LFFN=O(1), wFFN=2D+6, κ=O(τ),\displaystyle L_{\rm FFN}=O(1),\text{ }w_{\rm FFN}=2D+6,\text{ }\kappa=O\left(\tau\right),

such that on the good event ℰ\mathcal{E} defined in (34), it satisfies for the low-rank linear oracle kernel 𝒦\mathcal{K} defined in (17),

𝔼𝔰f​[ℛ𝔰f​(T∗)−2​ℛ𝔰f​(𝒦)|ℰ]≤36​C1​k​τ2​β2​b6n+4​C2​k​r​σ2​τ4​b8n2,\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}({{\rm T}}^{*})-2\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\mathcal{K})|\mathcal{E}\right]\leq\frac{36C_{1}k\tau^{2}\beta^{2}b^{6}}{n}+\frac{4C_{2}kr\sigma^{2}\tau^{4}b^{8}}{n^{2}},

where the good event ℰ\mathcal{E} occurs with probability no less than 1−8​k​exp⁡(−3​n16​b2​τ​(6​b2​τ+1))1-8k\exp\left(-\frac{3n}{16b^{2}\tau(6b^{2}\tau+1)}\right). The constants C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} hide the dependency on some absolute constants.

The proof of Lemma 4 is deferred to Appendix D.3.

6.2 Approximation Error of the Low-rank Linear Kernel Algorithm

Our goal in this subsection is to show in Lemma 5, under the good event ℰ\mathcal{E}, the low-rank linear kernel oracle 𝒦⁡(𝔰)\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s}) is accurate.

Lemma 5.

Suppose the input satisfies Assumption 2 and the target function class satisfies Assumption 1. Then under Setting 1 and for good event ℰ\mathcal{E} defined in (34), it satisfies

𝔼𝔰f​[ℛ𝔰f​(𝒦)|ℰ]≤18​C1​k​τ2​β2​b6n+8​r​σ2​τ2​b4n.\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\mathcal{K})|\mathcal{E}\right]\leq\frac{18C_{1}k\tau^{2}\beta^{2}b^{6}}{n}+\frac{8r\sigma^{2}\tau^{2}b^{4}}{n}.

The constant C1C_{1} hides the dependency on some absolute constants.

The proof of Lemma 5 is deferred to Appendix D.4.

6.3 Transformer-based ICL Generalization Error for Low-rank Linear Functions

Building on the error bounds established in Sections 6.1 and 6.2, we derive a bound on the mean squared generalization error for the low-rank linear model (16) in the ICL setting.

Theorem 1.

Suppose the target function class satisfies Assumption 1 and the input satisfies Assumption 2. Then under Setting 1, if the transformer network class 𝒯\mathcal{T} is chosen with parameters

de​m​b​e​d=2D+6, ℓ=n+1, LT=2, mT=1,\displaystyle d_{embed}=2D+6,\text{ }\ell=n+1,\text{ }L_{\rm T}=2,\text{ }m_{\rm T}=1, (35)
LFFN=O(1), wFFN=2D+6, κ=O(τ),\displaystyle L_{\rm FFN}=O(1),\text{ }w_{\rm FFN}=2D+6,\text{ }\kappa=O\left(\tau\right),

where O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) hides the dependency on the absolute constants. For n≥Θ⁡(τ2​b4)n\geq\Theta(\tau^{2}b^{4}) up to a logarithmic factor, the empirical risk minimizer T^\widehat{{\rm T}} defined in (9) satisfies the mean squared generalization error bound:

ℛ⁡(T^)≤(72​C1​k​τ2​β2​b6n+16​C2​r​σ2​τ2​b4n)+C3​(D​log⁡(n​D​Γ)Γ),\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(\widehat{{\rm T}})\leq\left(\frac{72C_{1}k\tau^{2}\beta^{2}b^{6}}{n}+\frac{16C_{2}r\sigma^{2}\tau^{2}b^{4}}{n}\right)+C_{3}\left(\frac{D\log(nD\Gamma)}{\sqrt{\Gamma}}\right), (36)

The constants C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} hide the absolute constants, and C3C_{3} hides the dependency on b,βb,\beta.

Our generalization error bound in Theorem 1 also connects to the multi-task learning literature. The approximation rate obtained in bai2023transformers and zhang2024trained is O⁡(D/n)O(D/n), which scales with the ambient dimension DD. Exploiting a shared low-dimensional structure in the function space, tripuraneni2021provable and du2021few improve this to O⁡(r/n)O(r/n). The dominating term in our bound is O⁡(k/n)O(k/n) with k≤rk\leq r, reflecting the additional gain from the interplay between the shared representation WW and the input data XX.

7 ICL Generalization Error for Multi-index Model

In this section, we study the approximation error I{\rm I} and II{\rm II} for the multi-index model ℱMI,U\mathcal{F}_{{\rm MI},U} in the ICL setup. We first show that the transformer can implement the anisotropic kernel estimator 𝒦⁡(𝔰)\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s}) in (20), and then we bound its mean squared generalization error ℛ⁡(T^)\mathcal{R}(\widehat{{\rm T}}).

We make the following assumptions on the function (task) space and the distribution of the input.

Assumption 3 (Function Class).

Let α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1], R,L,b>0R,L,b>0, Ω=[−b,b]D\Omega=[-b,b]^{D}. For a fixed U∈ℝD×rU\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times r} with orthonormal columns, we consider the multi-index function (task) space

ℱ=ℱMI,U:={f:Ω→ℝ |\displaystyle\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}_{{\rm MI},U}:=\{f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\text{ }| ​f​(𝐱)=g⁡(U⊤​𝐱)​ for some ​α​-Hölder ​g:ℝr→ℝ​ with Hölder constant\displaystyle\text{ }f(\mathbf{x})=g(U^{\top}\mathbf{x})\text{ for some }\alpha\text{-H\"{o}lder }g:\mathbb{R}^{r}\to\mathbb{R}\text{ with H\"{o}lder constant}
no larger than L, and ∥f∥L∞​(Ω)≤R}\displaystyle\text{ no larger than }L,\text{ and }\|f\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq R\}

We let ρf\rho_{f} be a probability distribution on ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Assumption 4 (Input Distribution).

Let Ω=[−b,b]D\Omega=[-b,b]^{D} with b>0b>0, and let U∈ℝD×rU\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times r} have orthonormal columns. For any 𝐱∈Ω\mathbf{x}\in\Omega and h>0h>0, define Bh​(𝐱):={𝐳∈Ω:‖U⊤​𝐳−U⊤​𝐱‖2≤h}B_{h}(\mathbf{x}):=\left\{\mathbf{z}\in\Omega:\|U^{\top}\mathbf{z}-U^{\top}\mathbf{x}\|_{2}\leq h\right\}. We assume that the input distribution ρ𝐱\rho_{\mathbf{x}} is supported within Ω\Omega and that there exist uniform constants Cρ,1,Cρ,2,h0>0C_{\rho,1},C_{\rho,2},h_{0}>0 such that

Cρ,1​hr≤ρ𝐱​(Bh​(𝐱))≤Cρ,2​hrC_{\rho,1}h^{r}\leq\rho_{\mathbf{x}}(B_{h}(\mathbf{x}))\leq C_{\rho,2}h^{r}

for all 𝐱∈supp⁡(ρ𝐱)\mathbf{x}\in\operatorname{supp}(\rho_{\mathbf{x}}) and 0<h≤h00<h\leq h_{0}.

Our goal next is to bound the errors I{\rm I} and II{\rm II} in Section 7.1 and Section 7.2 on the good event ℰ\mathcal{E}. Then we combine all the errors to get an error bound for ℛ⁡(T^)\mathcal{R}(\widehat{\rm T}) in Section 7.3.

7.1 Transformer Implements Anisotropic Kernel Estimator

We first establish that the error term II{\rm II} in (25) is zero by showing that the transformer can exactly implement anisotropic kernel estimator.

Mainly, we follow the idea in shen2025understanding, but extend it to the anisotropic case. We first utilize the interaction mechanism of attention to construct several layers of Transformer. This connection between the attention mechanism and kernel estimator can be rigorously established. More precisely, we show that transformers can implement the anisotropic kernel estimator exactly, without any approximation error. We state this result as in Lemma 6. Such connection between anisotropic kernel and transformer can also be validated by numerical experiments in Section 4.2. The complete proof of Lemma 6 is deferred to Appendix D.5.

Lemma 6.

Suppose the target function class satisfies Assumption 3 and the input satisfies Assumption 4. Then under Setting 1, there exists a transformer network T∗∈𝒯{\rm T}^{*}\in\mathcal{T} with parameters

de​m​b​e​d=2D+6, ℓ=n+1, LT=4, mT=n,\displaystyle d_{embed}=2D+6,\text{ }\ell=n+1,\text{ }L_{\rm T}=4,\text{ }m_{\rm T}=n,
LFFN=O(1), wFFN=2D+6, κ=O(D8n2b8R4/h8)\displaystyle L_{\rm FFN}=O(1),\text{ }w_{\rm FFN}=2D+6,\text{ }\kappa=O\left({D^{8}n^{2}b^{8}R^{4}}/{h^{8}}\right)

such that for any prompt 𝔰f\mathfrak{s}_{f}, it satisfies for the anisotropic oracle kernel 𝒦\mathcal{K} defined in (20),

T∗​(𝔰f)=𝒦⁡(𝔰f).{\rm T}^{*}(\mathfrak{s}_{f})=\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s}_{f}). (37)

The notation O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) hides absolute constants.

Remark 2 (Universality).

In Lemma 4 and Lemma 6, the network architecture and weight parameters of the constructed transformer T∗{{\rm T}}^{*} are independent of different target function ff and input 𝔰\mathfrak{s}. This construction demonstrates that the transformers can universally implement or approximate the corresponding kernel algorithm.

Lemma 6 establishes that the error term II{\rm II} in (25) is zero. It is worthwhile to note that although our analysis focuses only on the multi-index model, the result extends naturally to a broader class of models, e.g., single-index model or isotropic regular function model, with little additional effort.

7.2 Approximation Error of the Anisotropic Kernel Algorithm

As demonstrated in Lemma 6, transformer can exactly implement the anisotropic kernel estimator with zero approximation error, i.e., error term II{\rm II} equal to zero. Our next result in Lemma 7 shows the bound on error term I{\rm I}, which is the error given by oracle kernel algorithm. We defer the proof of Lemma 7 to Appendix D.6.

Lemma 7.

Suppose the target function class satisfies Assumption 3 and the input satisfies Assumption 4. Then under Setting 1, it satisfies

𝔼𝔰f​[ℛ𝔰f​(𝒦)]≤C3​([log⁡(h−1)]1+3​r2n​hr+h2​α​[log⁡(h−1)]2).\mathbb{E}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\mathcal{K})\right]\leq C_{3}\left(\frac{\left[\log\left(h^{-1}\right)\right]^{1+\frac{3r}{2}}}{nh^{r}}+h^{2\alpha}[\log(h^{-1})]^{2}\right). (38)

The constant C3C_{3} hides the constants depending on r,b,D,L,R,Cρ,1,Cρ,2r,b,D,L,R,C_{\rho,1},C_{\rho,2}.

LFFN=O(1), wFFN=2D+6, κ=O(D8n4​α+2​r+82​α+rb8R4),\displaystyle L_{\rm FFN}=O(1),\text{ }w_{\rm FFN}=2D+6,\text{ }\kappa=O\left(D^{8}n^{\frac{4\alpha+2r+8}{2\alpha+r}}b^{8}R^{4}\right),

∎

8 Conclusion and Discussions

In this work, we demonstrated that transformers can act as adaptive and anisotropic algorithmic learners in context, extending the kernel perspective on ICL beyond the isotropic setting considered in prior work. Our numerical experiments revealed a strong alignment between the attention patterns of trained transformers and the underlying anisotropic kernels, suggesting that attention can adapt to the low-dimensional and direction-dependent structure shared across tasks. Motivated by these empirical observations, we developed a theoretical framework for both low-rank linear regression and anisotropic kernel regression. We established generalization error bounds demonstrating that transformers can implicitly implement these learning algorithms even in the presence of noisy responses. We further provided explicit constructions of wide and shallow transformer architectures that perform inference solely through prompt conditioning without parameter updates. Together, our empirical and theoretical results suggest that attention goes beyond measuring similarities in the raw input space: it can capture task-dependent geometric structure and exploit intrinsic low-dimensional information that isotropic kernels may fail to capture.

Limitations and future directions.

While our analysis establishes representational and generalization guarantees for transformer-based ICL, it does not address whether gradient-based training can provably recover the proposed constructions. Future research could investigate the optimization dynamics of transformers, characterize the trade-off between depth and width, and extend the framework to settings with local task-dependent anisotropic structures. Such extensions would provide a more comprehensive understanding of the adaptability and robustness of transformers as in-context algorithmic learners.

Appendix C Further Details on the Experiments

For the transformer architecture used in the experiments for ℱLinear,W\mathcal{F}_{{\rm Linear},W} in Section 4.1, we fix a linear transformer with hyperparameters de​m​b​e​d=8d_{embed}=8, LT=2L_{\rm T}=2, LFNN=6L_{\rm FNN}=6. The length of the prompt is chosen with n=16n=16 and the number of attention heads is m=1m=1 for each layer. We generate Γ=50000\Gamma=50000 for both training and testing. The model is trained with batch size 100100, using Adam with learning rate 0.0010.001 for 100100 epochs. The testing MSE for model in ℱLinear,W\mathcal{F}_{{\rm Linear},W} is 8.3×10−58.3\times 10^{-5}, and relative error is 2.0×10−22.0\times 10^{-2}.

For the transformer architecture used in the experiments for ℱMI,U\mathcal{F}_{{\rm MI},U} in Section 4.2, we fix a transformer (last layer with softmax activation and all previous layers with ReLU activations) with hyperparameters de​m​b​e​d=8d_{embed}=8, LT=4L_{\rm T}=4, LFNN=6L_{\rm FNN}=6. The length of the prompt is chosen with n=16n=16 and the number of attention heads is m=1m=1 for each layer. We generate Γ=50000\Gamma=50000 for both training and testing. The model is trained with batch size 100100, using Adam with learning rate 0.0010.001 for 100100 epochs. The kernel bandwidth is fixed at h=1h=1. The testing MSE for the model in ℱMI,U\mathcal{F}_{{\rm MI},U} is 2.3×10−32.3\times 10^{-3}, and relative error is 8.2×10−28.2\times 10^{-2}.

and

D.4 Proof of Lemma 5

D.6 Proof of Lemma 7

Proof of Lemma 7.

The main idea for proving Lemma 7 is to decompose it into:

ℛ𝔰f​(𝒦)=(𝒦⁡(𝔰f)−f⁡(𝐱n+1))2\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathfrak{s}_{f}}(\mathcal{K})=\left(\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s}_{f})-f(\mathbf{x}_{n+1})\right)^{2} =(𝒦⁡(𝔰f)−𝒦¯​(f,𝐱n+1)+𝒦¯​(f,𝐱n+1)−f⁡(𝐱n+1))2\displaystyle=\left(\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s}_{f})-\bar{\mathcal{K}}(f;\mathbf{x}_{n+1})+\bar{\mathcal{K}}(f;\mathbf{x}_{n+1})-f(\mathbf{x}_{n+1})\right)^{2} (54)
≤2​(𝒦⁡(𝔰f)−𝒦¯​(f,𝐱n+1))2⏟A1+2​(𝒦¯​(f,𝐱n+1)−f⁡(𝐱n+1))2⏟A2\displaystyle\leq 2\underbrace{\left(\mathcal{K}(\mathfrak{s}_{f})-\bar{\mathcal{K}}(f;\mathbf{x}_{n+1})\right)^{2}}_{\rm A1}+2\underbrace{\left(\bar{\mathcal{K}}(f;\mathbf{x}_{n+1})-f(\mathbf{x}_{n+1})\right)^{2}}_{\rm A2}

where the error in A1{\rm A1} measures the variance of kernel estimator, A2{\rm A2} measures the bias of using kernel estimator to approximate the target function ff. Here 𝒦⁡(⋅)\mathcal{K}(\cdot) is given by (20), and 𝒦¯​(⋅)\bar{\mathcal{K}}(\cdot) is the integral form of kernel estimator:

𝒦¯​(f,𝐱n+1):\displaystyle\bar{\mathcal{K}}(f;\mathbf{x}_{n+1}): =𝔼𝐱,ϵ​[Kh​(U⊤​𝐱n+1−U⊤​𝐱)​(f⁡(𝐱)+ϵ)]𝔼𝐱​[Kh​(U⊤​𝐱n+1−U⊤​𝐱)]\displaystyle=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\epsilon}\left[K_{h}(U^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-U^{\top}\mathbf{x})(f(\mathbf{x})+\epsilon)\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}\left[K_{h}(U^{\top}\mathbf{x}_{n+1}-U^{\top}\mathbf{x})\right]} (55)

where Kh​(𝐱):=e−‖𝐱‖2h2K_{h}(\mathbf{x}):=e^{-\frac{\|\mathbf{x}\|^{2}}{h^{2}}}. By abusing the notation, we use d​𝐱d\mathbf{x} and d​ρ𝐱d{\rho}_{\mathbf{x}} interchangeably throughout this proof.

∙\bullet Bounding the bias A2{\rm A2}
By (54) and (55), the bias term A2{\rm A2} satisfies

For 𝐱\mathbf{x} close to the center 𝐱n+1\mathbf{x}_{n+1}, we use the Lipschitz property of ff to estimate the bias; For 𝐱\mathbf{x} far from the center 𝐱n+1\mathbf{x}_{n+1}, we use the Gaussian tail to bound the bias.

Let us consider the set of points in Ω\Omega which are at most h~\widetilde{h} distance to 𝐱n+1\mathbf{x}_{n+1} after projecting to the subspace UU:

Appendix E Other Definitions and Lemmas

We state the fundamental lemmas being used in this paper, with their proofs provided in shen2025understanding.

Lemma 8 (Interaction Lemma).

Let H=[ht]1≤t≤ℓ∈ℝde​m​b​e​d×ℓH=[h_{t}]_{1\leq t\leq\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{embed}\times\ell} be an embedding matrix such that ht(de​m​b​e​d−2):(de​m​b​e​d−1)=ℐth_{t}^{(d_{embed}-2):(d_{embed}-1)}=\mathcal{I}_{t} and htde​m​b​e​d=1h^{d_{embed}}_{t}=1. Fix 1≤t1,t2≤ℓ,1≤i≤de​m​b​e​d1\leq t_{1},t_{2}\leq\ell,1\leq i\leq d_{embed}, and ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in\mathbb{N}. Suppose de​m​b​e​d≥5d_{embed}\geq 5 and ‖H‖∞,∞<U\|H\|_{\infty,\infty}<U for some U>0U>0, and the data kernels Qd​a​t​a∈ℝ(de​m​b​e​d−3)×de​m​b​e​dQ^{data}\in\mathbb{R}^{(d_{embed}-3)\times d_{embed}} (the first (de​m​b​e​d−3)(d_{embed}-3) rows in the query matrix QQ) and Kd​a​t​a∈ℝ(de​m​b​e​d−3)×de​m​b​e​dK^{data}\in\mathbb{R}^{(d_{embed}-3)\times d_{embed}} (the first (de​m​b​e​d−3)(d_{embed}-3) rows in the key matrix KK) satisfy max⁡{‖Qd​a​t​a‖∞,∞,‖Kd​a​t​a‖∞,∞}≤κ\max\{\|Q^{data}\|_{\infty,\infty},\|K^{data}\|_{\infty,\infty}\}\leq\kappa. Then one can construct an attention head AA with ReLU activation (σ=ReLU\sigma={\rm ReLU}) such that

[A⁡(H)]t={σ⁡(⟨Qd​a​t​a​ht,Kd​a​t​a​ht2⟩)​𝐞iif ​t=t1,0otherwise.[A(H)]_{t}=\begin{cases}\sigma(\langle Q^{data}h_{t},K^{data}h_{t_{2}}\rangle)\mathbf{e}_{i}&\text{if}\text{ }t=t_{1},\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\\ \end{cases}

The weight parameters of this attention head satisfies ‖θA‖∞=O⁡(de​m​b​e​d4​κ2​ℓ2​U2)\|\theta_{A}\|_{\infty}=O(d_{embed}^{4}\kappa^{2}\ell^{2}U^{2}).

Lemma 9 (Gating Lemma).

Let de​m​b​e​d≥5d_{embed}\geq 5 and H=[ht]1≤t≤ℓ∈ℝde​m​b​e​d×ℓH=[h_{t}]_{1\leq t\leq\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{embed}\times\ell}, be an embedding matrix such that ht(de​m​b​e​d−2):(de​m​b​e​d−1)=(ℐt1,ℐt2)=ℐth_{t}^{(d_{embed}-2):(d_{embed}-1)}=(\mathcal{I}_{t}^{1},\mathcal{I}_{t}^{2})=\mathcal{I}_{t} and htde​m​b​e​d=1h^{d_{embed}}_{t}=1. Then for any r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} with 1≤r1≤r2≤de​m​b​e​d−31\leq r_{1}\leq r_{2}\leq d_{embed}-3 and any k1,k2k_{1},k_{2} with 1≤k1,k2≤ℓ1\leq k_{1},k_{2}\leq\ell, there exist both two-layer feed-forward networks (FFN)({\rm FFN}) such that

FFN1​(ht)={htif ​t∈{1,⋯,k1}[(ht)1(ht)r1−1𝟎(ht)r2+1(ht)de​m​b​e​d−3ℐt1ℐt21]otherwise \text{\rm FFN}_{1}(h_{t})=\begin{cases}h_{t}&\text{if}\text{ }t\in\{1,\cdots,k_{1}\}\\ \begin{bmatrix}(h_{t})_{1}\\ \vdots\\ (h_{t})_{r_{1}-1}\\ \mathbf{0}\\ (h_{t})_{r_{2}+1}\\ \vdots\\ (h_{t})_{d_{embed}-3}\\ \mathcal{I}_{t}^{1}\\ \mathcal{I}_{t}^{2}\\ 1\end{bmatrix}&\text{otherwise}\text{ }\\ \end{cases} (63)

and

FFN2​(ht)={htif ​t∈{k2,⋯,ℓ}[(ht)1(ht)r1−1𝟎(ht)r2+1(ht)de​m​b​e​d−3ℐt1ℐt21]otherwise \text{\rm FFN}_{2}(h_{t})=\begin{cases}h_{t}&\text{if}\text{ }t\in\{k_{2},\cdots,\ell\}\\ \begin{bmatrix}(h_{t})_{1}\\ \vdots\\ (h_{t})_{r_{1}-1}\\ \mathbf{0}\\ (h_{t})_{r_{2}+1}\\ \vdots\\ (h_{t})_{d_{embed}-3}\\ \mathcal{I}_{t}^{1}\\ \mathcal{I}_{t}^{2}\\ 1\end{bmatrix}&\text{otherwise}\text{ }\\ \end{cases} (64)

Additionally, we have ‖θFFN‖∞≤O⁡(ℓ​‖H‖∞,∞)\|\theta_{\rm FFN}\|_{\infty}\leq O(\ell\|H\|_{\infty,\infty}).

Lemma 10 (Decrementing Lemma).

Let de​m​b​e​d≥5d_{embed}\geq 5 and H=[ht]1≤t≤ℓ∈ℝde​m​b​e​d×ℓH=[h_{t}]_{1\leq t\leq\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{embed}\times\ell}, be an embedding matrix such that ht(de​m​b​e​d−2):(de​m​b​e​d−1)=(ℐt1,ℐt2)=ℐth_{t}^{(d_{embed}-2):(d_{embed}-1)}=(\mathcal{I}_{t}^{1},\mathcal{I}_{t}^{2})=\mathcal{I}_{t} and htde​m​b​e​d=1h^{d_{embed}}_{t}=1. Then for any r1,r2r_{1},r_{2} with 1≤r1≤r2≤de​m​b​e​d−31\leq r_{1}\leq r_{2}\leq d_{embed}-3 and any k1,k2k_{1},k_{2} with 1≤k1,k2≤ℓ1\leq k_{1},k_{2}\leq\ell and any M>0M>0, there exists a six-layer residual feed-forward network (FFN)({\rm FFN}) such that

FFN​(ht)+ht={htif ​t∈{1,⋯,k1}∪{k2,⋯,ℓ}[(ht)1(ht)r1−1(ht)r1−M(ht)r2−M(ht)r2+1(ht)de​m​b​e​d−3ℐt1]otherwise \text{\rm FFN}(h_{t})+h_{t}=\begin{cases}h_{t}&\text{if}\text{ }t\in\{1,\cdots,k_{1}\}\cup\{k_{2},\cdots,\ell\}\\ \begin{bmatrix}(h_{t})_{1}\\ \vdots\\ (h_{t})_{r_{1}-1}\\ (h_{t})_{r_{1}}-M\\ \vdots\\ (h_{t})_{r_{2}}-M\\ (h_{t})_{r_{2}+1}\\ \vdots\\ (h_{t})_{d_{embed}-3}\\ \mathcal{I}_{t}\\ 1\end{bmatrix}&\text{otherwise}\text{ }\\ \end{cases}

Additionally, we have ‖θFFN‖∞≤O⁡(ℓ​M)\|\theta_{\rm FFN}\|_{\infty}\leq O(\ell M).

Lemma 11 (Dudley Entropy Integral (c.f. [dudley1967sizes])).

Let {ξi}i=1n∈{−1,+1}\{\xi_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\in\{-1,+1\} be i.i.d Rademacher random variables. Suppose supf∈ℱ‖f‖L∞≤M\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\|f\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq M for some M>0M>0 and some function class ℱ\mathcal{F}. Then

𝔼{xi}i=1n,{ξi}i=1n[supf∈ℱ1n∑i=1nξif(xi)]≤infϵ>0(2ϵ+12n∫ϵMlog𝒩(δ,ℱ,∥⋅∥L∞) dδ).\mathbb{E}_{\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n},\{\xi_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}}\left[\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_{i}f(x_{i})\right]\leq\inf_{\epsilon>0}\left(2\epsilon+\frac{12}{\sqrt{n}}\int_{\epsilon}^{M}\sqrt{\log\mathcal{N}(\delta,\mathcal{F},\|\cdot\|_{L^{\infty}})}\text{ }d\delta\right). (65)

where 𝒩(δ,𝒯,∥⋅∥L∞)\mathcal{N}(\delta,\mathcal{T},\|\cdot\|_{L^{\infty}}) is the δ\delta-covering number of ℱ\mathcal{F} with respect to L∞L^{\infty} norm.

Definition 5.

Let {ϵi}i=1n\{\epsilon_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} be i.i.d Gaussian random variables. The Gaussian complexity of a function class ℋ\mathcal{H} over a set ZZ is defined as

𝒢Z​(ℋ):=1n​𝔼{ϵi}i=1n​suph∈ℋ[∑i=1nϵi​h​(zi)].\mathcal{G}_{Z}(\mathcal{H}):=\frac{1}{n}\mathbb{E}_{\{\epsilon_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}}\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}h(z_{i})\right]. (66)

Our next lemma bounds the Gaussian complexity by Rademacher complexity.

Lemma 12.

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a hypothesis space and Z={z1,⋯,zm}Z=\{z_{1},\cdots,z_{m}\}. Then

𝒢Z​(ℋ)≤2​log⁡(m)​RadZ​(ℋ)\mathcal{G}_{Z}(\mathcal{H})\leq 2\sqrt{\log(m)}{{\rm Rad}}_{Z}(\mathcal{H}) (67)
Proof.

Suppose ϵ=(ϵ1,⋯,ϵm)\bm{\epsilon}=(\epsilon_{1},\cdots,\epsilon_{m}) where ϵi\epsilon_{i} are i.i.d drawn from standard Gaussian distribution, and 𝝃=(ξ1,⋯,ξm)\bm{\xi}=(\xi_{1},\cdots,\xi_{m}) where ξi\xi_{i} are i.i.d drawn from Rademacher distribution. Then

𝒢Z​(ℋ):\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{Z}(\mathcal{H}): =1m​𝔼ϵ​[suph∈ℋ∑i=1mϵi​h​(zi)]=1m​𝔼𝝃,ϵ​[suph∈ℋ∑i=1m|ϵi|​ξi​h​(zi)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\epsilon}}\left[\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\epsilon_{i}h(z_{i})\right]=\frac{1}{m}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\xi},\bm{\epsilon}}\left[\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}|\epsilon_{i}|\xi_{i}h(z_{i})\right]
=1m𝔼ϵ[𝔼𝝃[suph∈ℋ∑i=1m|ϵi|ξih(zi)  ϵ]]≤1m𝔼ϵ∥ϵ∥∞𝔼𝝃[suph∈ℋ∑i=1mξih(zi)]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\epsilon}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\xi}}\left[\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}|\epsilon_{i}|\xi_{i}h(z_{i})\text{ }\vline\text{ }\bm{\epsilon}\right]\right]\leq\frac{1}{m}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\epsilon}}\|\bm{\epsilon}\|_{\infty}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\xi}}\left[\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\xi_{i}h(z_{i})\right]
≤1m⋅2​log⁡m⋅𝔼𝝃​[suph∈ℋ∑i=1mξi​h​(zi)]=2​log⁡m⋅RadZ​(ℋ).\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{m}\cdot 2\sqrt{\log m}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\xi}}\left[\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\xi_{i}h(z_{i})\right]=2\sqrt{\log m}\cdot{{\rm Rad}}_{Z}(\mathcal{H}).

where we have used the fact that, for large mm, 𝔼ϵ​‖ϵ‖∞≤2​log⁡m\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\epsilon}}\|\bm{\epsilon}\|_{\infty}\leq 2\sqrt{\log m} in the last inequality. ∎

Lemma 13 (Davis-Kahan Theorem [davis1970rotation, yu2015useful]).

Let A,A~∈ℝn×nA,\widetilde{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} be symmetric matrices with spectral decompositions

A=∑i=1nλi​ui​ui⊤,A~=∑i=1nλ~i​u~i​u~i⊤,A=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}u_{i}u_{i}^{\top},\qquad\widetilde{A}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\widetilde{\lambda}_{i}\widetilde{u}_{i}\widetilde{u}_{i}^{\top},

where λ1≥λ2≥⋯≥λn\lambda_{1}\geq\lambda_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_{n} are the eigenvalues of AA with orthonormal eigenvectors u1,…,unu_{1},\dots,u_{n}, and λ~1≥⋯≥λ~n\widetilde{\lambda}_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\widetilde{\lambda}_{n} are the eigenvalues of A~\widetilde{A} with orthonormal eigenvectors u~1,…,u~n\widetilde{u}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{u}_{n}. Let

E=A~−AE=\widetilde{A}-A

denote the perturbation. Fix an integer 1≤k≤n1\leq k\leq n, and let

U1=[u1,…,uk]∈ℝn×k,U~1=[u~1,…,u~k]∈ℝn×kU_{1}=[u_{1},\dots,u_{k}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k},\qquad\widetilde{U}_{1}=[\widetilde{u}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{u}_{k}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}

be the matrices whose columns span, respectively, the top-kk eigenspace of AA (associated with eigenvalues λ1,…,λk\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{k}) and the top-kk eigenspace of A~\widetilde{A} (associated with eigenvalues λ~1,…,λ~k\widetilde{\lambda}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{\lambda}_{k}). Suppose λk−λ~k+1>0\lambda_{k}-\widetilde{\lambda}_{k+1}>0. Then

‖U1​U1⊤−U~1​U~1⊤‖op≤‖E‖opλk−λ~k+1.\left\|U_{1}U_{1}^{\top}-\widetilde{U}_{1}\widetilde{U}_{1}^{\top}\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\frac{\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\lambda_{k}-\widetilde{\lambda}_{k+1}}.
Lemma 14 (Matrix Bernstein [tropp2015matrix]).

Let S1,…,SnS_{1},\ldots,S_{n} be independent, centered random matrices with common dimension d1×d2d_{1}\times d_{2}, and assume that:

𝔼⁡[Sk]=0​ and ​‖Sk‖2≤L​ for each ​k=1,…,n.\mathbb{E}[S_{k}]=0\text{ and }\left\|S_{k}\right\|_{2}\leq L\text{ for each }k=1,\ldots,n.

Introduce the random matrix

Y=∑k=1nSkY=\sum_{k=1}^{n}S_{k}

and let v⁡(Y)v(Y) denote the matrix variance statistic of the sum:

v⁡(Y)\displaystyle v(Y) =max⁡{‖𝔼⁡[Y​Y∗]‖2,‖𝔼⁡[Y∗​Y]‖2}\displaystyle=\max\left\{\left\|\mathbb{E}\left[YY^{*}\right]\right\|_{2},\left\|\mathbb{E}\left[Y^{*}Y\right]\right\|_{2}\right\}
=max⁡{‖∑k=1n𝔼⁡[Sk​Sk∗]‖2,‖∑k=1n𝔼⁡[Sk∗​Sk]‖2}.\displaystyle=\max\left\{\left\|\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[S_{k}S_{k}^{*}\right]\right\|_{2},\left\|\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbb{E}\left[S_{k}^{*}S_{k}\right]\right\|_{2}\right\}.

Then for all t≥0t\geq 0,

ℙ{∥Y∥2≥t}≤(d1+d2)⋅exp(−t2/2v⁡(Y)+L​t/3).\mathbb{P}\{\|Y\|_{2}\geq t\}\leq\left(d_{1}+d_{2}\right)\cdot\exp\left(\frac{-t^{2}/2}{v(Y)+Lt/3}\right).

Furthermore,

𝔼​‖Y‖2≤2​v​(Y)​log⁡(d1+d2)+13​L​log⁡(d1+d2).\mathbb{E}\|Y\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{2v(Y)\log\left(d_{1}+d_{2}\right)}+\frac{1}{3}L\log\left(d_{1}+d_{2}\right).
Lemma 15 (Intrinsic Matrix Bernstein [tropp2015matrix]).

Let S1,…,SnS_{1},\ldots,S_{n} be independent, centered random matrices with common dimension, and assume that:

𝔼⁡[Sk]=0​ and ​‖Sk‖2≤L​ for each ​k=1,…,n.\mathbb{E}[S_{k}]=0\text{ and }\left\|S_{k}\right\|_{2}\leq L\text{ for each }k=1,\ldots,n.

Introduce the random matrix

Y=∑k=1nSkY=\sum_{k=1}^{n}S_{k}

Let V1,V2V_{1},V_{2} be semidefinite upper bounds for the matrix-valued variances Var1​(Y){\rm Var}_{1}(Y) and Var2​(Y){\rm Var}_{2}(Y):

V1≽Var1​(Y)=𝔼⁡[Y​Y∗]=∑k=1n[Sk​Sk∗]andV2≽Var2​(Y)=𝔼⁡[Y∗​Y]=∑k=1n[Sk∗​Sk].V_{1}\succcurlyeq{\rm Var}_{1}(Y)=\mathbb{E}[YY^{*}]=\sum_{k=1}^{n}[S_{k}S_{k}^{*}]\quad\text{and}\quad V_{2}\succcurlyeq{\rm Var}_{2}(Y)=\mathbb{E}[Y^{*}Y]=\sum_{k=1}^{n}[S_{k}^{*}S_{k}].

Define an intrinsic dimension bound and a variance bound

d=intdim​[V100V2]:=tr⁡(V1)+tr⁡(V2)vandv:=max⁡{‖V1‖2,‖V2‖2}.d={\rm intdim}\begin{bmatrix}V_{1}&0\\ 0&V_{2}\end{bmatrix}:=\frac{{\rm tr}(V_{1})+{\rm tr}(V_{2})}{v}\quad\text{and}\quad v:=\max\{\|V_{1}\|_{2},\|V_{2}\|_{2}\}.

Then, for all t≥v+L/3t\geq\sqrt{v}+L/3,

ℙ{∥Y∥2≥t}≤4d⋅exp(−t2/2v+L​t/3).\mathbb{P}\{\|Y\|_{2}\geq t\}\leq 4d\cdot\exp\left(\frac{-t^{2}/2}{v+Lt/3}\right).

The next lemma states that, in the symmetric case, the perturbation of pseudo-inverse can be bounded by the perturbation of the original matrix.

Lemma 16.

Let A,B∈ℝr×rA,B\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r} be rank k<rk<r symmetric matrices. Then

‖B†−A†‖2≤3​max⁡{‖A†‖22,‖B†‖22}​‖B−A‖2\|B^{\dagger}-A^{\dagger}\|_{2}\leq 3\max\{\|A^{\dagger}\|^{2}_{2},\|B^{\dagger}\|_{2}^{2}\}\|B-A\|_{2}
Proof.

Write E:=B−AE:=B-A, α=λk​(A),β=λk​(B)\alpha=\lambda_{k}(A),\beta=\lambda_{k}(B). Let PA=A​A†,PB=B​B†P_{A}=AA^{\dagger},P_{B}=BB^{\dagger}. Notice that since A,BA,B are symmetric, we have A​A†=A†​AAA^{\dagger}=A^{\dagger}A and B​B†=B†​BBB^{\dagger}=B^{\dagger}B. Next, we make use of the identity

B†−A†=−B†​E​A†+(B†)2​E​(I−PA)+(I−PB)​E​(A†)2,B^{\dagger}-A^{\dagger}=-B^{\dagger}EA^{\dagger}+(B^{\dagger})^{2}E(I-P_{A})+(I-P_{B})E(A^{\dagger})^{2}, (68)

which can be verified in the following way:

The first term on the right-hand-side equals to

−B†​E​A†=−B†​(B−A)​A†=−B†​B​A†+B†​A​A†=−PB​A†+B†​PA.-B^{\dagger}EA^{\dagger}=-B^{\dagger}(B-A)A^{\dagger}=-B^{\dagger}BA^{\dagger}+B^{\dagger}AA^{\dagger}=-P_{B}A^{\dagger}+B^{\dagger}P_{A}.

Notice that A⁡(I−PA)=A−A​A†​A=0A(I-P_{A})=A-AA^{\dagger}A=0. The second term on the right-hand-side equals to

(B†)2​E​(I−PA)=(B†)2​(B−A)​(I−PA)=(B†)2​B​(I−PA)=B†​(I−PA).(B^{\dagger})^{2}E(I-P_{A})=(B^{\dagger})^{2}(B-A)(I-P_{A})=(B^{\dagger})^{2}B(I-P_{A})=B^{\dagger}(I-P_{A}).

Similarly, the third term on the right-hand-side equals to

(I−PB)​E​(A†)2=(I−PB)​(B−A)​(A†)2=−(I−PB)​A​(A†)2=−(I−PB)​A†.(I-P_{B})E(A^{\dagger})^{2}=(I-P_{B})(B-A)(A^{\dagger})^{2}=-(I-P_{B})A(A^{\dagger})^{2}=-(I-P_{B})A^{\dagger}.

Adding all three terms together gives B†−A†B^{\dagger}-A^{\dagger}.

Taking the operator norm on both sides of (68), and by using the fact ‖I−PA‖2=‖I−PB‖2=1\|I-P_{A}\|_{2}=\|I-P_{B}\|_{2}=1, it gives

‖B†−A†‖2\displaystyle\|B^{\dagger}-A^{\dagger}\|_{2} ≤‖B†‖2​‖E‖2​‖A†‖2+‖B†‖22​‖E‖2+‖E‖2​‖A†‖22\displaystyle\leq\|B^{\dagger}\|_{2}\|E\|_{2}\|A^{\dagger}\|_{2}+\|B^{\dagger}\|^{2}_{2}\|E\|_{2}+\|E\|_{2}\|A^{\dagger}\|^{2}_{2}
=(‖B†‖2​‖A†‖2+‖B†‖22+‖A†‖22)​‖E‖2\displaystyle=(\|B^{\dagger}\|_{2}\|A^{\dagger}\|_{2}+\|B^{\dagger}\|^{2}_{2}+\|A^{\dagger}\|^{2}_{2})\|E\|_{2}
≤3​max⁡{‖A†‖22,‖B†‖22}​‖B−A‖2\displaystyle\leq 3\max\{\|A^{\dagger}\|^{2}_{2},\|B^{\dagger}\|_{2}^{2}\}\|B-A\|_{2}

as desired. ∎
